items.responseText: Seasonal monsoon winds reversed, so merchants timed outward and return trips. A compass gave direction and an astrolabe estimated latitude. Planning and navigation made longer trading voyages more dependable.
Merchants waited for predictable winds to return home. A magnetic needle showed direction; larger hulls carried more cargo. Planned returns and these tools increased how much could be exchanged.
Monsoons helped trade. Sailors had a compass.
Monsoon winds, compass, astrolabe, larger ships.
Monsoon winds always blew west, never reversed, so nobody could sail home. The compass controlled rainfall and the astrolabe created wind.
Seasonal winds could be predicted, letting sailors schedule both journeys. Compass and astrolabe.
Wind seasons helped merchants plan trips out and back. A compass helped them find direction, allowing more reliable long-distance trade.
Monsoon patterns let merchants time return voyages. An astrolabe estimated latitude and bigger ships carried more goods. These made longer routes and larger cargo shipments possible.

Sailors worked out the yearly changes in prevailing winds to arrange round trips. Direction-finding needles and larger cargo vessels helped them stay on course and transport more goods over long routes.
Predictable monsoons guided departure dates. Gunpowder and paper money are my two maritime technologies; they made ships carry more cargo.
The compass showed direction and larger ships carried more cargo, allowing longer voyages and more goods to move.
Knowing monsoons let sailors schedule departures and returns. A compass pointed north and an astrolabe found latitude. But neither planning nor these tools changed the risk, reach or amount of trade.
The seasonal winds reversed every year so merchants could plan return trips. They never changed direction at any time. Compass and astrolabe helped navigation.

I disagree with saying monsoons never changed. Their seasonal reversal let ships return on schedule. Compass navigation and larger ships carrying more cargo supported regular trade over longer routes.

Knowing the yearly wind reversals let merchants plan both directions. A lateen sail helped vessels sail across varying wind angles and a compass helped sailors maintain direction. Those advantages made longer ocean trading voyages practical.
Seasonel winds change so merchants plan returns. A compas tells direction; big ships fit more goods. This makes long trade trips reliable and raises cargo volume.
I will explain the winds, then add my second technology when I finish.
Seasonal reversals allowed planned returns, while compasses gave direction and larger ships carried more cargo, making trade regular and extensive.

Malacca grew powerful by collecting revenue at its strategic strait as more merchants used the port. Ming admiral Zheng He visited Indian Ocean ports, increasing diplomatic and cultural contacts within that expanding network.
